I've been lucky enough to survive a few incidents where the odds were against it. Each time was very different in terms of what went through my mind.

The first time was surreal. The way I remember it was like watching it happen, but not being the one calling the shots. I was not thinking about what to do, my body just reacted. On auto-pilot or pure instinct. From my perspective it was like I was just an observer without any input.

Future unfortunate situations I did have input, but it still wasn't full manual control. More like being the coach and calling the plays.

How does you're brain/body react when it thinks it is about to die?

Edit:
From a reoccurring theme in the comments I have decided to never take up rock-climbing.
Have you ever had a moment in life where you knew your chances of surviving the next few minutes were very low?

Collapsed both lungs and broke ribs in a climbing accident, I remember almost making it back to the car, then waking up in the ICU. That moment when the vision tunnel started closing, I knew I was going to pass out and I remember wondering if the tree I was looking at was the last thing I would ever see. That was it though, nothing crazy.
Drowning in the beach but I kept the calm and someone came to rescue me.
Maybe I'm alone in this, but I suspect many people who answer "yes" to the question aren't particularily keen to talk about it.

That may be for some. But I am asking more about how their brain handled it, rather than the incident itself.
I'm not too keen on talking about some of my experiences, but this type of conversation doesn't bother me.

I find it interesting how people handle it in very different ways.

I think the largest variable is time of exposure to the threat. If I have been presented with some kind of acute threat that could unexpectedly take my life in a moment, the automatic reactions kick in.

However, being exposed to a life threatening event over hours or days, when you have time to reflect on what is occurring and evaluate your life... Well it changes something in you more than what is easy to explain by internet forum. Closest thing I've come to seeing another person express it is in Joseph Conrad's work.

I've never thought about that side of it. I can see how it would be very different. I never had time to think things through in a life threatening situation. It's always been a "Surprise, you're dead" thing for me.

I think in a lot of ways it would just be worse the longer it was prolonged.

Length of exposure to the threat and perceived intensity of the threat seem to be the two key factors.

Even "surprise you're dead" moments can mess a person up if they fixate on the event retrospectively in an unhealthy way.

Nothing wrong with any of it though. I think it does a person good to come face to face with their mortality here and there as long as it isn't recklessness for its own sake. But you go to some other countries and you can see public cremations going on all the time, on what are effectively pallet fires. In the West we have everything so sanitized and compartmentalized that only specific professions ever have to deal with death (and they deal with it disproportionately to the rest of society). So out here most people are so unfamiliar with it that they catch a glimpse of death and it shatters their psyche. Instead of experiencing post-traumatic growth they demand safer and safer spaces. The conditions SJWs start popping up in.

Well put. People who've never left the first world have no idea. None at all. You can tell them what you've seen, and they laugh because they think you're making it up. Death is some abstract, clinical concept aside from the odd mortician, physician, or emergency worker.

You'd be surprised. The first time you nearly get yourself killed, it can be traumatizing. After the first few times, you start to realize how fragile and precious human life is and want to remind people to /enjoy this, because you have no idea how lucky you are/.

One time I decided to swim alongside my tube instead of in it while in some river rapids. I was young!
